source_references.title: Software Engineering 2014: Curriculum Guidelines for Undergraduate Degree Programs in Software Engineering
source_references.locator: Chapter 4, §4.7, pp. 26–27: SEEK knowledge areas include requirements analysis and specification, software design, software verification and validation, software process, software quality, and security. §4.5, pp. 25–26, cautions that knowledge-area ordering does not prescribe curriculum sequencing and identifies quality/security as cross-cutting concerns.

source_references.claim_limit: These are knowledge areas, not an officially mandated subgroup taxonomy or proof that each should become a separate student-facing specialization. The recommended groupings below are an internal synthesis, not an ACM/IEEE-endorsed taxonomy.

source_references.title: European Cybersecurity Skills Framework Role Profiles
source_references.locator: Twelve profiles include CISO, Cyber Legal/Policy/Compliance Officer, Cybersecurity Architect, Cybersecurity Implementer, Cybersecurity Researcher, Cybersecurity Risk Manager, Cyber Incident Responder, Digital Forensics Investigator, Penetration Tester, Cybersecurity Auditor, Cybersecurity Educator, and Cyber Threat Intelligence Specialist. ENISA's ESCO crosswalk distinguishes exact, broader and partial task matches.
source_references.supports: Independent EU-wide corroboration of distinct practice functions corresponding to governance, architecture/implementation, offensive testing, operations/response, investigation/forensics, audit/risk and threat analysis.
source_references.claim_limit: ECSF is a European role/profile framework, not a global specialization taxonomy. Its 12 profiles are roles, not 12 areas of specialization; they are used only as cross-checks on functional boundaries, not copied into subgroups.

source_references.title: CISSP Certification Exam Outline
source_references.locator: Eight knowledge domains: Security and Risk Management; Asset Security; Security Architecture and Engineering; Communication and Network Security; Identity and Access Management; Security Assessment and Testing; Security Operations; Software Development Security. The outline details assessment/testing, incident operations, forensics, secure development and recovery topics.
source_references.supports: An internationally offered professional certification body treats governance/risk, architecture, networks, identity, testing, operations and secure development as substantial distinguishable cybersecurity knowledge domains.
source_references.claim_limit: These are CISSP exam domains, not necessarily standalone university majors, occupational titles or this product's exact AOS labels/count. CISSP is an experienced-professional certification; its blueprint must not be presented as an entry-level curriculum or credential requirement.

source_references.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology, NICE initiative
source_references.title: NICE Cybersecurity Workforce Framework (NIST SP 800-181 overview)
source_references.locator: Framework defines Category as high-level grouping, Specialty Area as an area of concentrated work/function, and Work Role as detailed tasks and KSAs; named categories include Oversee & Govern, Protect & Defend, Analyze, Investigate, Collect & Operate, Operate & Maintain, and Securely Provision.
source_references.supports: There are distinct concentrated cybersecurity work functions, including governance, defense, analysis/investigation, operations and secure provisioning. This is particularly relevant to defining area-of-specialization boundaries.
source_references.claim_limit: The cited 2017 overview is an older US workforce-framework summary, not an academic subgroup standard or globally binding taxonomy. NICE category/specialty/work-role hierarchy must not be copied directly or confused with this student AOS taxonomy.

source_references.title: Platform Engineering Maturity Model
source_references.locator: Sections 'What is platform engineering?' and 'How to use this model', lines 14-27 of the web edition: platform engineering plans and provides computing platforms; its aspects are independently evaluated and implementations vary by organization.
source_references.supports: Independent CNCF elaboration that platform engineering is a coherent specialization area and that platform implementations are contextual rather than a rigid universal checklist.
source_references.claim_limit: The maturity model is not an academic accreditation standard, fixed subgroup-count rule, vendor-neutral role taxonomy, or evidence for assigning this repository's specific roles.

source_references.publisher: Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), Platforms Working Group and TAG App Delivery contributors
source_references.title: Platforms White Paper for Cloud Native Computing
source_references.locator: Overview and linked white paper: internal platforms provide common capabilities and services to application/product teams; the paper addresses platform capabilities, outcomes, measurement and platform-team success.
source_references.supports: Platform engineering is a distinct cloud-native practice area focused on providing reusable internal capabilities and developer-facing platform services, rather than a synonym for infrastructure operations or all DevOps work.
source_references.claim_limit: This is practitioner guidance and does not mandate a student taxonomy, establish a universal profession/licensure scheme, or justify assigning any repository role to a specialization.

source_references.title: FinOps Framework Phases
source_references.locator: Inform, Optimize and Operate phases, especially lines 101-131 of the web edition: technology cost/usage visibility, optimization, and collaborative action across engineering, finance and business teams.
source_references.supports: Cloud cost/usage optimization is an important capability connected to cloud engineering and operation.
source_references.claim_limit: FinOps is cross-technology and cross-functional, not a cloud-only specialization; it should not become a D005 subgroup solely because cloud spend is one application. The framework does not define D005 role membership.

source_references.title: What is Site Reliability Engineering?
source_references.locator: 'What is Site Reliability Engineering?' and 'What we do as SRE' sections: reliability work applies software engineering to operations and focuses on availability, latency, performance, capacity, and running production systems.
source_references.supports: Cloud service reliability and production operations are a recognizable, task-distinct area, not merely another name for building infrastructure or authoring deployment pipelines.
source_references.claim_limit: Google's practice is an influential industry example, not a global academic standard, universal organizational model, employment guarantee, or role-to-domain mapping authority.

source_references.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
source_references.title: NIST Cloud Computing Reference Architecture
source_references.locator: Section 2.1, printed pp. 3-4 / PDF pp. 9-10, identifies cloud consumer, provider, carrier, auditor and broker actors; Appendix A, printed pp. 20-21 / PDF pp. 26-27, defines SaaS, PaaS and IaaS. Section 3 describes provider-side service orchestration, resource abstraction/control, physical resources and service management.
source_references.supports: Cloud architecture, infrastructure/service provision, and cloud service operations are materially different concerns; IaaS/PaaS/SaaS are service models and the actor taxonomy is a reference architecture, not learner specialization labels.

source_references.locator: Section 5, 'Software components in CMSIS-Packs': describes embedded software as modular systems built from components such as middleware, source code, libraries and example projects targeted to microcontroller families/platforms.
source_references.supports: Microcontroller/embedded firmware development is a coherent device-level technical area with its own platform and component constraints, distinct from integrating complete networked IoT systems.

source_references.publisher: European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI), with IoT/edge standards community contributors
source_references.title: Enabling Multi-access Edge Computing in the IoT: How to deploy ETSI MEC and oneM2M
source_references.locator: Introduction and Figure 1, printed pp. 4-5: distinguishes IoT devices/things, edge nodes/network edge, core network and cloud data center; describes moving compute/data hosting toward the edge for latency and bandwidth needs. The paper's objective is to connect ETSI MEC and oneM2M standardization/deployment concerns.
source_references.supports: Edge computing is a distinct systems-design concern about where compute and data hosting occur and how edge services interoperate with IoT architectures; it is not just another name for embedded firmware or IoT architecture as a whole.
source_references.claim_limit: ETSI is a European standards organization and the paper is practitioner/standards integration guidance, not a global academic taxonomy, mandated subgroup count, or proof that edge should be a standalone specialization in every IoT domain.

source_references.locator: ISO's public abstract and edition information; the 2024 second edition describes a standardized IoT reference architecture with a common vocabulary, reusable designs and implementation patterns. Public online table of contents for the edition lists foundational, business, usage, functional, trustworthiness and construction viewpoints, plus construction patterns.
source_references.supports: IoT system architecture is a distinct design concern involving multiple viewpoints and construction patterns, not simply device programming or a list of application sectors.
source_references.claim_limit: The public abstract/table of contents does not prescribe student specializations, a role taxonomy, subgroup count, or membership of any repository role. The full standard is not freely available through this listing.

source_references.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Cyber-Physical Systems Public Working Group
source_references.title: Framework for Cyber-Physical Systems: Volume 1, Overview (NIST SP 1500-201)
source_references.locator: Abstract and framework summary: CPS joins interacting digital, analog, physical and human components; engineering facets are conceptualization, realization and assurance; concerns include functional behavior, trustworthiness, timing, data, composition, boundaries and lifecycle. Identifies application sectors separately from engineering concerns.
source_references.supports: Embedded/CPS engineering has device/physical-system constraints and lifecycle/assurance concerns that are not reducible to IoT service integration. Sector labels are applications, not necessarily specialization areas.
source_references.claim_limit: The framework is a systems-analysis framework, not an occupational standard, academic accreditation, fixed specialization count, or direct role mapping authority.

source_references.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
source_references.title: NIST SP 800-183, Networks of 'Things'
source_references.locator: NIST publication abstract: identifies sensing, computing, communication and actuation as core primitives of IoT/network-of-things systems; applies to distributed systems with scale, heterogeneity, temporal, reliability and security concerns.
source_references.supports: IoT spans interacting device and network functions; sensing/actuation are system functions and should not be confused with a complete learner specialization by themselves.
source_references.claim_limit: This 2016 NIST technical model is not a global academic curriculum, specialization taxonomy, occupational classification, or source for assigning specific roles.

areas_of_specialization.label: IoT Architecture and Systems Integration

areas_of_specialization.boundary: Design and connect IoT devices, gateways, communications, data services and applications into a coherent system, addressing functional interactions, interoperability, lifecycle and trustworthiness concerns.

source_references.title: Arm Keil MDK Getting Started Guide, software components in CMSIS-Packs

source_references.supports: Microcontroller/embedded firmware development is a coherent device-level technical area with its own platform and component constraints, distinct from integrating complete networked IoT systems.
source_references.claim_limit: Vendor documentation is illustrative implementation guidance, not a vendor-neutral international standard, academic taxonomy, formal role definition, or evidence for any role's placement.

source_references.publisher: European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI), with IoT/edge standards community contributors
source_references.title: Enabling Multi-access Edge Computing in the IoT: How to deploy ETSI MEC and oneM2M
source_references.locator: Introduction and Figure 1, printed pp. 4-5: distinguishes IoT devices/things, edge nodes/network edge, core network and cloud data center; describes moving compute/data hosting toward the edge for latency and bandwidth needs. source_references.claim_limit: ETSI is a European standards organization and the paper is practitioner/standards integration guidance, not a global academic taxonomy, mandated subgroup count, or proof that edge should be a standalone specialization in every IoT domain.

source_references.claim_limit: This is curriculum guidance, not a universal professional taxonomy, accreditation of a particular specialization model, or role-to-area mapping evidence.

source_references.publisher: Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) and IEEE Computer Society curriculum task force
source_references.title: Computing Curricula 2023 � Human-Computer Interaction Core
source_references.locator: HCI-A Understanding the User (needs-finding and user-centered methods); HCI-C Accessibility and Inclusive Design; HCI-D Evaluating the Design; HCI-E System Design and prototyping. The page states these are HCI knowledge units in a computing curriculum.
source_references.supports: User research/understanding, evaluation, interaction/system design, and accessibility/inclusive design are recognized as distinguishable HCI knowledge areas. This provides an international academic basis for separating the proposed branches.
source_references.claim_limit: Curriculum knowledge units are not automatically occupational specializations, and the framework does not prescribe this product's labels/count or determine individual role fit.

source_references.title: ISO 9241-210:2019 Ergonomics of human-system interaction � Part 210: Human-centred design for interactive systems

Page confirms 2019 edition remains current after 2025 review.
source_references.supports: Human-centred design is a lifecycle practice with user and usability concerns broader than visual UI production alone.
source_references.claim_limit: The public abstract does not prescribe UX subgroups, exact specialization count, job titles, or this catalogue's role assignments.

source_references.title: About the Usability Body of Knowledge
source_references.locator: Mission and project description: a living, broad and inclusive reference for usability practice, intended to collate published literature, conference proceedings and practitioner knowledge; the organization notes the field is multidisciplinary.

source_references.claim_limit: The project page is not a completed consensus specialization taxonomy or formal accreditation standard and cannot establish the proposed count on its own.

source_references.publisher: World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), Web Accessibility Initiative
source_references.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1

source_references.claim_limit: WCAG defines conformance requirements for web content, not a career taxonomy, credential, or evidence that accessibility should be isolated from general design responsibilities.

source_references.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1

areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Computing Curricula 2023 � Human-Computer Interaction Core

areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: Curriculum knowledge units are not automatically occupational specializations, and the framework does not prescribe this product's labels/count or determine individual role fit.

source_references.claim_limit: A future-network framework is not a prescribed specialization or evidence that every listed technology deserves a separate subgroup.

source_references.publisher: Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) Data Science Task Force
source_references.title: Computing Competencies for Undergraduate Data Science Curricula — Draft 2, Chapter 3
source_references.locator: Chapter 3, §3.1: lists Analysis and Presentation; Data Acquisition, Management and Governance; Data Mining; Machine Learning; Big Data Systems, and other computing knowledge areas; notes mathematics/statistics competencies and at least one application-domain context are also needed.
source_references.supports: Provides an independently locatable decomposition of core data-science knowledge and supports grouping the candidate areas around coherent competencies rather than existing role counts.

source_references.title: Computing Competencies for Undergraduate Data Science Curricula � Draft 2, Chapter 3
source_references.locator: Chapter 3, �3.1: lists Analysis and Presentation; Data Acquisition, Management and Governance; Data Mining; Machine Learning; Big Data Systems, and other computing knowledge areas; notes mathematics/statistics competencies and at least one application-domain context are also needed.
source_references.supports: Provides an independently locatable decomposition of core data-science knowledge and supports grouping the candidate areas around coherent competencies rather than existing role counts.
source_references.claim_limit: This is a curricular report/draft, not a settled occupational taxonomy; topics overlap, and exact groupings for this student-facing product remain synthesis.

source_references.publisher: Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) Data Science Task Force
source_references.title: Computing Competencies for Undergraduate Data Science Curricula: Final Report
source_references.locator: Body of Knowledge / Knowledge Areas and report methodology: task force drew on academic and industry surveys, public drafts, broad community feedback, and a global advisory group; its knowledge areas include Data Acquisition, Management and Governance; Analysis and Presentation; Big Data Systems; Data Mining; Machine Learning; and related computing foundations.
source_references.supports: Data-science education recognizes distinct but related competencies in data stewardship/systems, analysis/presentation, data mining and machine learning. The report explicitly treats a complete data-science curriculum as interdisciplinary.
source_references.claim_limit: Computing curriculum knowledge areas are not occupations or a universal professional specialization taxonomy; the report itself calls for broader multidisciplinary collaboration and does not mandate this product's four-area count.

source_references.publisher: Association for Computing Machinery, IEEE Computer Society and Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence
source_references.title: Computer Science Curricula 2023: Final Report
source_references.locator: CS2023 Knowledge Model discussion: Data Science was considered as a separate knowledge area but not retained; CS-specific topics are distributed across AI, Graphics and Interactive Techniques, Data Management, and Mathematical and Statistical Foundations.
source_references.supports: Cautions against treating data science as a single isolated technical bucket and supports making overlap with AI/ML, data management, visualization and mathematical/statistical foundations explicit.
source_references.claim_limit: CS2023 is a computer-science curriculum rather than a complete data-science occupational model; its decision does not imply Data Science is not a distinct interdisciplinary domain.

source_references.publisher: Association for Computing Machinery (ACM) and Association for Information Systems (AIS)
source_references.title: IS 2010 Curriculum Guidelines for Undergraduate Degree Programs in Information Systems
source_references.locator: Data, Information and Knowledge Management material: data quality, OLTP versus OLAP, business intelligence, data warehousing and data mining; includes learning outcomes for creating a simple data warehouse/data mart and explaining the relationship among these concepts.
source_references.supports: Separates the BI information foundation (warehouse/OLAP) from analytic use/mining and situates both in organizational information systems.
source_references.claim_limit: An IS curriculum is not a universal occupational taxonomy and does not prescribe these three areas or determine role links.

source_references.title: DAMA-DMBOK 2.0 Revised: Infographics / Knowledge Areas
source_references.locator: Knowledge-area map lists Data Warehousing and Business Intelligence separately from Data Architecture, Data Modeling and Design, Data Storage and Operations, Data Integration and Interoperability, Metadata Management and Data Quality Management.
source_references.supports: BI has an identifiable professional knowledge area connected to, but not identical with, architecture, integration, modeling, storage and quality practices.
source_references.claim_limit: A body-of-knowledge map is not a student specialization taxonomy; it does not prescribe this product's labels or count, nor prove individual role fit.

source_references.title: DAMA-DMBOK Revision
source_references.locator: 2024 revision description: maintenance release; overarching data-management framework and knowledge areas retained, with terminology/structure clarifications.
source_references.supports: Confirms the DMBOK knowledge-area framework remains maintained and that BI sits within a broader data-management ecosystem.
source_references.claim_limit: Does not by itself establish a job taxonomy or specialization count.

source_references.title: TDWI Analytics Maturity Model Assessment
source_references.locator: Assessment description: analytics deployments mature beyond spreadsheets/dashboards toward self-service and organizational capability; the framework assesses analytics-program dimensions and decision/use of analytics.
source_references.supports: Distinguishes BI delivery/reporting from broader organizational analytics capability and its use in decisions.
source_references.claim_limit: A maturity model evaluates organizations/programmes, not individuals or a universal specialization taxonomy.

source_references.publisher: Transforming Data With Intelligence (TDWI), in partnership with the Institute for Certification of Computing Professionals (ICCP)
source_references.title: Overview of the Certified Business Intelligence Professional Certification
source_references.locator: CBIP scope lists BI (dashboards, reporting, visualization), analytics, data management (modeling, quality, integration), data architecture (warehouse/marts/lakes/metadata), and strategy/program methods. The guide is described as the basis for examination scope.
source_references.supports: Professional BI practice spans reporting/visualization, data foundations, analytics and program strategy, corroborating the need for distinct but connected areas.
source_references.claim_limit: TDWI's certification scope is intentionally broad and overlaps data science, ML and AI; it is not an exclusive boundary rule or this catalogue's specialization count.

areas_of_specialization.label: Quantitative Pricing and Financial Engineering
areas_of_specialization.description: Use mathematical and computational models to value financial instruments and engineer financial products/strategies, including derivative valuation, numerical methods, calibration and model implementation.
areas_of_specialization.boundary: Use mathematical and computational models to value financial instruments and engineer financial products/strategies, including derivative valuation, numerical methods, calibration and model implementation.

source_references.title: CFA Program Candidate Body of Knowledge
source_references.locator: Quantitative Methods includes probability, regression, time series, AI/ML and big-data applications, backtesting/simulation/scenario analysis; portfolio topics include construction, execution, trading and market microstructure.
source_references.supports: Quantitative methods are used in investment analysis and portfolio decisions; systematic investment, execution and market microstructure form distinguishable applied concerns.
source_references.claim_limit: The CFA CBOK covers the broad investment profession, not only quantitative finance; it does not imply all listed topics are required in every quantitative-finance path or define this exact taxonomy.

source_references.title: Portfolio Mathematics (2026 Curriculum)
source_references.locator: Learning outcomes cover expected portfolio value, variance, standard deviation, covariance/correlation and shortfall-risk metrics; the reading connects quantitative portfolio mathematics to portfolio risk/return.
source_references.supports: Quantitative portfolio measurement and risk analysis are core, identifiable financial applications of mathematical methods.
source_references.claim_limit: Does not establish that portfolio analytics must be a separate specialization from investment/trading or risk modeling in this product.

source_references.title: CFA Program Curriculum Overview
source_references.locator: Curriculum structures quantitative methods, derivatives/risk management, portfolio construction, asset classes and specialized portfolio-management pathways as distinct topic areas.
source_references.supports: Financial valuation/risk and portfolio decision-making are related but distinguishable knowledge/application clusters.
source_references.claim_limit: CFA curriculum spans investment management broadly and does not prescribe a quantitative-finance-only area taxonomy.

source_references.title: Active Equity Investing: Strategies (2026 Curriculum)
source_references.locator: Summary and learning outcomes distinguish quantitative/systematic from fundamental/discretionary investing; describes factor, statistical-arbitrage and market-microstructure strategies, and quantitative workflow including data processing, backtesting, evaluation, portfolio construction, risk and trading-cost models.
source_references.supports: Systematic quantitative investment/trading is a coherent application area distinct from general financial modeling and risk quantification.
source_references.claim_limit: The reading is focused on active equity strategies and should not be generalized as a complete list of quant-finance specializations or a job taxonomy.

source_references.title: FRM Program Exams and Topic Areas
source_references.locator: 2026 exam topics: Part I Foundations of Risk Management, Quantitative Analysis, Financial Markets and Products, Valuation and Risk Models; Part II Market Risk, Credit Risk, Operational/Integrated Risk, Liquidity/Treasury Risk, and Risk/Investment Management.
source_references.supports: Quantitative methods and valuation models form a distinct foundation, with applied financial risk areas such as market, credit and liquidity risk; professional material also connects risk and investment management.
source_references.claim_limit: FRM is a risk-management curriculum, not a full quantitative-finance taxonomy; it does not set this product's subgroup count or prove any role mapping.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Active Equity Investing: Strategies (2026 Curriculum)
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: Summary and learning outcomes distinguish quantitative/systematic from fundamental/discretionary investing; describes factor, statistical-arbitrage and market-microstructure strategies, and quantitative workflow including data processing, backtesting, evaluation, portfolio construction, risk and trading-cost models.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Systematic quantitative investment/trading is a coherent application area distinct from general financial modeling and risk quantification.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: The reading is focused on active equity strategies and should not be generalized as a complete list of quant-finance specializations or a job taxonomy.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: FRM Program Exams and Topic Areas

areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: FRM is a risk-management curriculum, not a full quantitative-finance taxonomy; it does not set this product's subgroup count or prove any role mapping.

areas_of_specialization.label: Digital Payments and Transaction Systems
areas_of_specialization.description: Engineer digital payment products and the systems that initiate, route, process, clear, settle, reconcile and protect payment transactions, including payment interfaces and connections to payment infrastructure.

source_references.publisher: Bank for International Settlements, Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (BIS CPMI)
source_references.title: Payment Aspects of Financial Inclusion in the Fintech Era
source_references.locator: §2 taxonomy and §4.3 payment infrastructure: defines payment systems/instruments and describes front-end arrangements versus back-end processing/clearing/settlement; discusses fintech service models, payment access, infrastructure and platform dependencies.
source_references.supports: Payment engineering spans user/service initiation and back-end transaction processing/infrastructure, which can form a focused practice area.

source_references.publisher: Bank for International Settlements, Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (BIS CPMI)
source_references.title: Payment Aspects of Financial Inclusion in the Fintech Era
source_references.locator: �2 taxonomy and �4.3 payment infrastructure: defines payment systems/instruments and describes front-end arrangements versus back-end processing/clearing/settlement; discusses fintech service models, payment access, infrastructure and platform dependencies.
source_references.supports: Payment engineering spans user/service initiation and back-end transaction processing/infrastructure, which can form a focused practice area.
source_references.claim_limit: Report focuses on payments and financial inclusion; it is not a complete FinTech engineering curriculum, a universal product taxonomy, or a specialization-count mandate.

source_references.publisher: Bank for International Settlements, Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (BIS CPMI)
source_references.title: Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures � Overview
source_references.locator: Mandate and Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures section: international standards cover payment systems, central securities depositories, securities settlement systems, central counterparties and trade repositories; CPMI addresses safety/efficiency, oversight and digital innovation in payments, clearing and settlement.
source_references.supports: Payment systems and securities/market infrastructures are coherent, technically distinct systems with public international standards and operational properties.
source_references.claim_limit: The CPMI's remit is infrastructure policy/standards, not a learner taxonomy or all consumer-facing financial technology.

source_references.title: Financial Stability Implications from FinTech: Supervisory and Regulatory Issues that Merit Authorities' Attention
source_references.locator: Figure 1, 'Classification of selected FinTech innovations by economic function': payments/clearing/settlement; deposits/lending; capital raising; market support; investment management/investor services; insurance; and financial market infrastructure are shown as functions, while mobile/web, APIs/cloud, DLT, e-trading and other items are shown as innovations/enablers.
source_references.supports: A useful structural distinction for this domain: financial service/infrastructure functions differ from cross-cutting technologies used to deliver them.
source_references.claim_limit: The taxonomy is a 2017 supervisory overview of selected innovations, not a current complete occupational or specialization taxonomy and not a mandate for these three areas.

source_references.title: How Countries Can Expand Access to Digital Financial Services
source_references.locator: Report overview and linked technical notes: digital financial services, business models, infrastructure prerequisites, digital identity, open APIs and regulatory/policy issues across country contexts.
source_references.supports: Digital finance depends on shared infrastructure and interoperable interfaces, while service offerings and local regulatory implementation vary across jurisdictions.
source_references.claim_limit: The report is policy-oriented and emphasizes inclusion; it does not prescribe a universal FinTech engineering specialization set.

source_references.publisher: World Bank Group, Digital Finance Inclusion platform
source_references.title: Glossary of Key Digital Financial Services Terms: APIs and Open Banking
source_references.locator: API entries distinguish payment APIs, data APIs, ecosystem-expansion APIs, and consent/identity APIs; Open API section describes integration and testing/launch patterns and gives examples from several jurisdictions.
source_references.supports: APIs are an enabling integration layer that can support multiple financial product areas, rather than one finance service specialization by themselves.
source_references.claim_limit: Examples are jurisdiction- and provider-specific; they do not establish that every FinTech learner needs open-banking expertise or that legal permissions are globally uniform.

source_references.title: About the Casualty Actuarial Society
source_references.locator: Mission statement describes advancing actuarial science applied to general insurance, including property, casualty and similar risk exposures.
source_references.supports: General insurance/P&C is a coherent and substantial actuarial practice context, distinct from life, health and pension systems.
source_references.claim_limit: CAS has a P&C focus and cannot alone define a global actuarial taxonomy or establish boundaries for all other practices.

source_references.title: IAA Education Syllabus and Guidelines
source_references.locator: Education guidelines, especially breadth and elective-subject sections: actuarial education must cover core topics while associations may package or substitute electives differently; examples include health care and general insurance practice. The document notes commonality across education systems alongside local association discretion.
source_references.supports: There is a shared global actuarial foundation while specialist education and packaging may vary across associations and regions.
source_references.claim_limit: Education syllabus subject groupings do not directly establish student-facing practice taxonomy or role fit.

source_references.title: Forums Recommendations to Council
source_references.locator: Final recommendations table: Banking is described as an important emerging area of practice; Data Analytics is described as cross-practice and important but with mixed views about its organizational placement.
source_references.supports: Banking and data analytics are legitimate actuarial contexts/topics that merit monitoring, while data analytics is explicitly cross-cutting and banking is still characterized as emerging in this governance record.
source_references.claim_limit: This 2021 recommendation does not establish either as a universally settled core specialization; neither is made a seventh/eighth default branch in this review.

source_references.title: Forums
source_references.locator: Forum descriptions cover Banking; Data Analytics; Enterprise & Financial Risk; General Insurance (including non-life/P&C terminology across regions); Health; Inclusive Insurance; Mortality; and Pensions, Benefits & Social Security. The page describes the IAA as an association of national actuarial associations.
source_references.supports: Cross-regional recognition of the insurance, health, pension/social-security, enterprise/financial-risk, mortality and data-analytics contexts; terminology varies by region.
source_references.claim_limit: IAA forums vary in maturity and governance and are not all equivalent to established standalone specializations. Data analytics and banking are not asserted here as universal core branches.

source_references.title: Practice Areas
source_references.locator: Practice-area list: AI and emerging technologies; Finance and investment; General insurance; Health and care; Life; Pensions; Risk management; Sustainability; Cross-practice work. The page distinguishes focused practice areas from matters affecting multiple practices.
source_references.supports: Life, health, general insurance, pensions, investment/finance and risk management are recognized actuarial practice contexts; technology, sustainability and cross-practice work also exist but may cut across the core areas.
source_references.claim_limit: This is one professional body's practice-board structure, not a universal taxonomy or a required subgroup count. It does not determine the catalogue's role memberships.

source_references.title: FSA Flexible Pathway and Courses
source_references.locator: Pathway examples identify life and annuities, investment, retirement and health practice courses; the page explicitly illustrates both a single-practice pathway and a combined cross-practice pathway, with some courses marked jurisdiction-specific.
source_references.supports: Several recurring practice contexts are distinct yet can be combined by learners; jurisdiction-specific curriculum variants should not be presented as global requirements.
source_references.claim_limit: SOA pathways are one association's qualification design, not a complete global taxonomy or a prescription for this catalogue's exact six areas.

source_references.locator: Education guidelines, especially breadth and elective-subject sections: actuarial education must cover core topics while associations may package or substitute electives differently; examples include health care and general insurance practice. The document notes commonality across education systems alongside local association discretion.
source_references.supports: There is a shared global actuarial foundation while specialist education and packaging may vary across associations and regions.
source_references.claim_limit: Education syllabus subject groupings do not directly establish student-facing practice taxonomy or role fit.

source_references.title: Forums Recommendations to Council
source_references.locator: Final recommendations table: Banking is described as an important emerging area of practice; Data Analytics is described as cross-practice and important but with mixed views about its organizational placement.
source_references.supports: Banking and data analytics are legitimate actuarial contexts/topics that merit monitoring, while data analytics is explicitly cross-cutting and banking is still characterized as emerging in this governance record.
source_references.claim_limit: This 2021 recommendation does not establish either as a universally settled core specialization; neither is made a seventh/eighth default branch in this review.

source_references.title: Forums
source_references.locator: Forum descriptions cover Banking; Data Analytics; Enterprise & Financial Risk; General Insurance (including non-life/P&C terminology across regions); Health; Inclusive Insurance; Mortality; and Pensions, Benefits & Social Security. The page describes the IAA as an association of national actuarial associations.
source_references.supports: Cross-regional recognition of the insurance, health, pension/social-security, enterprise/financial-risk, mortality and data-analytics contexts; terminology varies by region.
source_references.claim_limit: IAA forums vary in maturity and governance and are not all equivalent to established standalone specializations. Data analytics and banking are not asserted here as universal core branches.

source_references.title: Practice Areas
source_references.locator: Practice-area list: AI and emerging technologies; Finance and investment; General insurance; Health and care; Life; Pensions; Risk management; Sustainability; Cross-practice work. The page distinguishes focused practice areas from matters affecting multiple practices.
source_references.supports: Life, health, general insurance, pensions, investment/finance and risk management are recognized actuarial practice contexts; technology, sustainability and cross-practice work also exist but may cut across the core areas.
source_references.claim_limit: This is one professional body's practice-board structure, not a universal taxonomy or a required subgroup count. It does not determine the catalogue's role memberships.

source_references.title: FSA Flexible Pathway and Courses
source_references.locator: Pathway examples identify life and annuities, investment, retirement and health practice courses; the page explicitly illustrates both a single-practice pathway and a combined cross-practice pathway, with some courses marked jurisdiction-specific.
source_references.supports: Several recurring practice contexts are distinct yet can be combined by learners; jurisdiction-specific curriculum variants should not be presented as global requirements.
source_references.claim_limit: SOA pathways are one association's qualification design, not a complete global taxonomy or a prescription for this catalogue's exact six areas.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.publisher: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, hosted by the Bank for International Settlements
areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Core Principles for effective banking supervision
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: BCP 01.1-02.3: de facto minimum standard and universal applicability. Principle 14, BCP40.32-33: corporate governance; Principle 15, BCP40.34: comprehensive, bank-wide risk management; Principle 17, BCP40.39: credit risk including the full credit life cycle; Principles 18-26: problem exposures, concentration, related parties, country/transfer, market, banking-book interest-rate, liquidity, operational risk/resilience and internal controls; Principle 29, BCP40.66: customer due diligence/abuse of financial services.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Risk, governance, operational resilience and financial-crime controls are broad, connected bank-wide supervisory dimensions; credit lifecycle is distinct enough to be specified separately. The Core Principles apply across bank types and jurisdictions.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: This is a supervisory framework describing expected bank controls and supervisor assessment, not a professional curriculum, occupational classification or student specialization count.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.publisher: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, hosted by the Bank for International Settlements
areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Principles for the Management of Credit Risk
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: Overview and table of contents, principles grouped into: (i) credit-risk environment; (ii) sound credit-granting process; (iii) credit administration, measurement and monitoring; (iv) adequate controls. The 2025 revised principles page describes these four evaluation areas.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Credit management comprises connected lifecycle/control activities and is not four independent banking specializations by default.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: The four elements are supervisory assessment areas for credit-risk management; copying them into subgroup records would confuse control dimensions with student-facing specialization taxonomy.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.publisher: Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (BIS) and International Organization of Securities Commissions
areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: Overview and scope; list of principles, including legal basis, governance, comprehensive risk management, settlement finality and money settlements. The overview defines covered infrastructures as payment systems, central securities depositories, securities settlement systems, central counterparties and trade repositories.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Payments, clearing and settlement infrastructures are a distinct technical/operational practice area with specialized standards and risks.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: The standards govern financial market infrastructures, not all bank payment-service workers; they do not prove that payments must be a separate specialization beneath D060 rather than a neighboring domain or an area within broader banking operations.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Credit & Lending Education and Training for Professional Bankers
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: PDF pp. 1-2, Overview/Scope: calls credit and lending a core area of banking and states the standard sets high-level education content without country-wise product/delivery detail; pp. 4-7, Key Aspects and Advanced Learners: sound lending, borrower/facility types, credit appraisal/risk, monitoring/impaired assets, with advanced export/project finance and portfolio topics.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Credit and lending is a coherent, separately teachable professional education area and can be considered as a distinct candidate subgroup under this parent.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: The standard guides member bodies and others; it explicitly leaves country-specific products/regulation to local context. It does not prescribe the subgroup structure/count for this catalogue or establish that every learner needs an advanced credit path.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Global Standards
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: Page lines/sections: introduction (states there are no definitive internationally agreed answers to all banker knowledge/skills questions); lines 6 and 15 (25 national institutes and international professional education aims); headings for the fourth standard, Credit & Lending, and sixth standard, Treasury Operations; lines 47 and 51 identify the treasury and operational-risk documents as first drafts.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Credit & Lending has a named GBEStB education standard; treasury operations has been proposed in a first-draft standard. The Board itself cautions that globally agreed answers to the full banker knowledge/skills question are not definitive.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: Voluntary professional education standards, not accreditation of a universal subgroup taxonomy. The treasury document is identified as a first draft.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: ABA Online Training Certificates: Retail Banking

areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: A distinct retail/personal banking education pathway with a coherent product, operations and customer-service boundary.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: U.S. professional association curriculum; supports a learning-area example, not a global taxonomy mandate.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: Professional training examples, not proof of a universal business-banking subgroup taxonomy.

source_references.publisher: Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology (ABET)
source_references.title: Criteria for Accrediting Engineering Technology Programs, 2026�2027
source_references.locator: Electrical/electronics program criteria enumerating circuit analysis/design, analog/digital electronics, microcomputers, and a choice of control, instrumentation, communications, computer, power or energy systems.
source_references.supports: Power/energy, electronics, communications, control, instrumentation and computer systems are distinct technical directions within electrical/electronic engineering education.
source_references.claim_limit: ABET criteria govern accredited programs in its system and list curricular options; they do not mandate this catalogue's number or exact labels and are not a global regulator.

source_references.publisher: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)
source_references.title: Electrical Engineering
source_references.locator: Overview sections on power and energy systems, signals/communications/electronics, and control systems/computing.
source_references.supports: IEEE describes power systems, electronics/semiconductors, communications/signal processing, and control/computing as substantial technical areas within the broad discipline.
source_references.claim_limit: The overview is a broad professional explainer, not an accreditation standard or required taxonomy/count; embedded/computer engineering overlaps with computing and other engineering domains.

source_references.title: Inspec Classification
source_references.locator: Inspec B-class Electrical Engineering and Electronics headings include communications (B60), instrumentation and special applications (B70), and power systems and applications (B80); control technology is separately classified under C30.
source_references.supports: The technical literature recognizes distinguishable electrical practice/research areas across communications, instrumentation, power systems and control.
source_references.claim_limit: A literature indexing scheme is not a student specialization taxonomy and its codes/count cannot be copied as subgroup structure.

source_references.publisher: Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology (ABET)
source_references.title: Criteria for Accrediting Engineering Programs, 2025�2026
source_references.locator: Mechanical and Similarly Named Engineering Programs section: engineering/science/math applied to modelling, analysis, design and realization of physical systems, components and processes; coverage of thermal and mechanical systems, with depth in at least one.
source_references.supports: Mechanical engineering has shared foundational methods but distinct thermal and mechanical system directions; the criteria support a broad parent with selectable depth rather than a single universal learner route.
source_references.claim_limit: ABET criteria apply within ABET accreditation and do not prescribe the catalogue's specialization count or globally mandatory curriculum.

source_references.title: Technical Division Pages
source_references.locator: Division scope statements for Design Engineering, Fluids Engineering, Heat Transfer, Manufacturing Engineering, Materials, Dynamic Systems and Control, Power, and related engineering areas.
source_references.supports: Mechanical engineering practice includes distinguishable design, fluids/thermal, manufacturing, materials and dynamic-systems directions with their own technical communities.
source_references.claim_limit: ASME divisions are professional communities and some are application-specific or cross-disciplinary; they are evidence of technical fields, not a ready-made learner taxonomy or role assignment.

source_references.title: Academic Accreditation Guidelines v4.1
source_references.locator: Appendix B examples of programmes considered for accreditation, including design, energy, manufacturing, materials, mechatronics, aerospace, automotive, building services and other mechanical-related fields.
source_references.supports: Cross-regional professional accreditation practice recognizes several coherent mechanical-engineering directions and multidisciplinary applications.
source_references.claim_limit: This is UK professional accreditation guidance and its illustrative degree list is not exhaustive, not a prescribed specialization count, and not authority to duplicate separate catalogue domains such as automotive engineering or industrial automation.

source_references.title: Specialty Certification Descriptions

source_references.claim_limit: This is one professional academy's certification structure, not a universal academic taxonomy; certification specialty labels are evidence of recognized practice, not a requirement that every area become a student subgroup. source_references.title: Criteria for Accrediting Engineering Programs, 2026�2027
source_references.locator: Environmental Engineering and Similarly Named Engineering Programs, curriculum criteria: material balances and fate/transport among air, water and soil; laboratories in more than one major focus area (examples air, water, land, environmental health); design of environmental engineering systems; public/private environmental responsibilities.

areas_of_specialization.label: Generalist and Primary Care
areas_of_specialization.description: Broad first-contact and continuing care across common conditions and life stages.
areas_of_specialization.boundary: Broad first-contact and continuing care across common conditions and life stages.

source_references.title: Classifying health workers: mapping occupations to the international standard classification
source_references.claim_limit: WHO's occupational groupings support distinctions among medical practice areas, not Sifter's complete taxonomy or any jurisdiction's scope-of-practice rules.
source_references.locator: 2019 mapping, ISCO 2211 Generalist medical practitioners; description of generalist diagnostic, treatment and referral responsibilities.
source_references.supports: Generalist medical practice is distinguished from specialist medical practice and supports first-contact, continuing-care scope.

areas_of_specialization.label: Adult Medical Specialties
areas_of_specialization.description: Non-surgical, system-focused diagnosis and treatment of adult disease, including internal-medicine subspecialties.
areas_of_specialization.boundary: Non-surgical, system-focused diagnosis and treatment of adult disease, including internal-medicine subspecialties.

source_references.title: Our structure
source_references.locator: Specialist Sections, Divisions, and Multidisciplinary Joint Committees; lists recognized European specialty sections and explains that divisions may represent a branch or competence.
source_references.supports: Medical specialties can be organized into sections, branches, and cross-specialty areas; jurisdictional arrangements differ.
source_references.geographic_scope: European professional framework, not a global or national licensing rule.

source_references.title: Classifying health workers: mapping occupations to the international standard classification
source_references.locator: 2019 publication, medical-doctor and specialist-doctor groupings; distinguishes medical specialties and surgical specialties and classifies health-worker occupations for international comparability.
source_references.supports: International health-workforce classification distinguishes specialist doctors from other health-worker occupations and groups specialties for statistics.
source_references.geographic_scope: International comparability classification; not a student-facing specialization taxonomy.

areas_of_specialization.label: Surgical and Procedural Specialties
areas_of_specialization.description: Specialties whose core practice uses operative or other procedural treatment.
areas_of_specialization.boundary: Specialties whose core practice uses operative or other procedural treatment.

source_references.title: Classifying health workers: mapping occupations to the international standard classification
source_references.locator: 2019 publication, medical-doctor and specialist-doctor groupings; distinguishes medical specialties and surgical specialties and classifies health-worker occupations for international comparability.
source_references.supports: International health-workforce classification distinguishes specialist doctors from other health-worker occupations and groups specialties for statistics.
source_references.geographic_scope: International comparability classification; not a student-facing specialization taxonomy.

areas_of_specialization.label: Emergency and Critical Care
areas_of_specialization.description: Time-critical stabilization, emergency assessment, intensive care, and acute deterioration management.
areas_of_specialization.boundary: Time-critical stabilization, emergency assessment, intensive care, and acute deterioration management.

source_references.title: Emergency care
source_references.locator: Overview: emergency care as an integrated platform for time-sensitive acute illness/injury; critical care as ongoing intensive treatment for life-threatening illness or injury.
source_references.supports: Emergency and critical care are distinct but connected service/practice areas for acute and life-threatening conditions.
source_references.claim_limit: WHO describes health-service scope, not a physician-specialty taxonomy or the exact Sifter area boundary.

areas_of_specialization.label: Maternal and Reproductive Medicine
areas_of_specialization.description: Pregnancy, childbirth, reproductive health, and related specialist medical care.
areas_of_specialization.boundary: Pregnancy, childbirth, reproductive health, and related specialist medical care.

source_references.title: WHO recommendations on maternal health: guidelines approved by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee, 2nd ed
source_references.locator: Overview: recommendations cover promotion, prevention and management of maternal complications during pregnancy, childbirth and postnatal periods.
source_references.supports: Maternal medicine is a coherent clinical practice scope spanning pregnancy, childbirth, postnatal care and complications.
source_references.claim_limit: Supports maternal-care scope, not all reproductive-medicine subfields, role assignment, licensing, or an exact area count.

areas_of_specialization.label: Child and Adolescent Medicine
areas_of_specialization.description: Medical care focused on newborn, child, and adolescent health and development.
areas_of_specialization.boundary: Medical care focused on newborn, child, and adolescent health and development.

source_references.title: Classifying health workers: mapping occupations to the international standard classification
source_references.claim_limit: WHO's occupational groupings support distinctions among medical practice areas, not Sifter's complete taxonomy or any jurisdiction's scope-of-practice rules.
source_references.locator: 2019 mapping, specialist medical practitioners: paediatrics and related specialties; definition focuses on infants, children and adolescents.
source_references.supports: Child and adolescent medical practice is identified as a patient-age/life-stage specialty grouping.

areas_of_specialization.label: Mental and Behavioural Medicine
areas_of_specialization.description: Medical assessment and treatment of mental, behavioural, and neuropsychiatric conditions.
areas_of_specialization.boundary: Medical assessment and treatment of mental, behavioural, and neuropsychiatric conditions.

source_references.title: Classifying health workers: mapping occupations to the international standard classification
source_references.claim_limit: WHO's occupational groupings support distinctions among medical practice areas, not Sifter's complete taxonomy or any jurisdiction's scope-of-practice rules.
source_references.locator: 2019 mapping, specialist medical practitioners: psychiatric specialties and related branches; definition covers mental illness and behavioural disorders.
source_references.supports: Psychiatric/mental and behavioural medical practice is distinguished as a specialty grouping.

areas_of_specialization.label: Diagnostic and Laboratory Medicine
areas_of_specialization.description: Physician-led pathology, laboratory, imaging, and diagnostic interpretation specialties; technical delivery roles remain in their own professional domains.
areas_of_specialization.boundary: Physician-led pathology, laboratory, imaging, and diagnostic interpretation specialties; technical delivery roles remain in their own professional domains.

source_references.title: Classifying health workers: mapping occupations to the international standard classification
source_references.claim_limit: WHO's occupational groupings support distinctions among medical practice areas, not Sifter's complete taxonomy or any jurisdiction's scope-of-practice rules.
source_references.locator: 2019 mapping, specialist medical practitioners: medical specialties include pathology, radiology, haematology and related diagnostic specialties.
source_references.supports: Physician diagnostic specialties are distinct from non-physician technical delivery occupations, consistent with this area's stated boundary.

areas_of_specialization.label: Preventive and Occupational Medicine
areas_of_specialization.description: Physician practice focused on prevention, occupational/environmental health, and population-level risk; broader public-health programme practice remains distinguishable from D026.
areas_of_specialization.boundary: Physician practice focused on prevention, occupational/environmental health, and population-level risk; broader public-health programme practice remains distinguishable from D026.

source_references.title: Classifying health workers: mapping occupations to the international standard classification
source_references.claim_limit: WHO's occupational groupings support distinctions among medical practice areas, not Sifter's complete taxonomy or any jurisdiction's scope-of-practice rules.
source_references.locator: 2019 mapping, specialist medical practitioners: medical group of specialties includes occupational medicine; see also preventive-medicine specialist examples.
source_references.supports: Preventive and occupational medicine are represented as medical practice specialties, distinct from general population-health programme roles.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Specialty and Subspecialty Certificates
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: Overview: specialty boards and fields; describes broad and focused scopes and subspecialty branches.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Physician specialty structures distinguish broad care areas, organ systems, patient groups, and treatments.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Medical specialties can be organized into sections, branches, and cross-specialty areas; jurisdictional arrangements differ.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Curricula
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: Approved postgraduate curricula page: specialty and subspecialty curricula, with curriculum list.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Specialties and subspecialties have distinct formal postgraduate curricula in the UK.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: International health-workforce classification distinguishes specialist doctors from other health-worker occupations and groups specialties for statistics.

source_references.locator: Eight sections listed: Academic pharmacy; Clinical biology; Community pharmacy; Health and medicines information; Hospital pharmacy; Industrial pharmacy; Military and emergency pharmacy; Social and administrative pharmacy. Last updated 24 September 2026.

source_references.title: Pharmaceutical practice and the sections
source_references.locator: The page lists eight practice sections: Academic pharmacy; Clinical biology; Community pharmacy; Health and medicines information; Hospital pharmacy; Industrial pharmacy; Military and emergency pharmacy; Social and administrative pharmacy. Page states FIP advances pharmacy practice across settings; page last updated 24 September 2026.
source_references.supports: These eight areas are internationally recognized FIP practice-interest sections and provide a global starting framework for coverage of distinct pharmacy practice contexts.
source_references.claim_limit: A universal official specialization taxonomy; legal or credential equivalence between countries; a claim that every area is a regulated specialty; or role membership in this catalogue.

source_references.title: Global Situation Report on Pharmacy 2025: Workforce, Practice and Policy
source_references.locator: PDF pp. 77-82, section 5, 'Advancing pharmacy specialisations': pp. 77-78 state there is no globally agreed definition; pp. 78-79 organize examples as traditional clinical/disease areas, service-based areas (e.g. pharmacovigilance, medication management/review, pharmaceutical public health), technical/system-based areas (e.g. regulatory science, informatics, policy), and emerging areas (e.g. digital pharmacy, AI, genomics, personalized medicine); pp. 79-82 discuss regional variation and limitations in comparable data.
source_references.supports: Pharmacy specializations may be organized by practice sector/activity and can include clinical, service, system and emerging areas; their recognition and credentials vary across regions.

source_references.title: Global competency and outcomes framework for the essential public health functions
source_references.locator: WHO publication overview: the framework provides international reference competencies and educational outcomes for the workforce delivering EPHFs; distinguishes context-adapted service/function identification, occupational workforce mapping and competency development.
source_references.supports: A global evidence base for workforce competencies and the broad range of public-health functions.
source_references.claim_limit: A fixed specialization count or a claim that occupation titles alone identify an individual's fit.

source_references.publisher: World Health Organization (WHO), Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), and World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH)
source_references.title: Competencies for One Health field epidemiology (COHFE) framework
source_references.locator: Framework overview lists 14 domains, including surveillance, field investigations, preparedness/response, epidemiological studies, data management/biostatistics/informatics, ecosystem health, leadership, community engagement, training and ethics; distinguishes human, animal and environmental sector-specific competencies.
source_references.supports: A globally co-developed One Health approach and distinct competency clusters for field epidemiology and response.
source_references.claim_limit: A claim that animal/environmental health roles automatically belong to the Public Health domain; task and parent-domain fit must be individually assessed.

source_references.title: Public health intelligence competency framework
source_references.locator: WHO framework dated 27 November 2025; overview describes technical domains detect, verify, analyse and assess plus collaborative information exchange; developed using literature review, job analyses, expert consultation and stakeholder surveys.
source_references.supports: Public-health intelligence is a coherent, task- and competency-defined specialization candidate spanning surveillance and health-threat decisions.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: The page names cellular pathology, cytology, clinical chemistry, haematology, immunology, medical microbiology, virology and transfusion science as specialist fields; it also notes emerging molecular biology, genomics and digital pathology. The linked discipline leaflet gives task-level descriptions for blood and cell sciences.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: These are established biomedical laboratory practice areas and help distinguish diagnostic disciplines by specimen, method and purpose.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: A globally fixed number, universal legal scope, or authority to assign every current D027 occupation to Biomedical Science. IBMS accreditation/registration context is UK-specific.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.publisher: International Federation of Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine (IFCC)
areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Clinical Chemistry and Laboratory Medicine: Role in Healthcare
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: Section 1.4 describes laboratory medicine as applying chemical, molecular and cellular concepts to health and disease, and discusses clinical chemistry, haematology, transfusion medicine, immunology, microbiology, toxicology and genetics. It states that the meaning/scope varies by country.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: A cross-nationally relevant evidence base for laboratory-medicine discipline boundaries and the overlap among them.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: One global subgroup count or identical licensing/occupational boundaries across jurisdictions.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.publisher: International Union of Basic and Clinical Pharmacology (IUPHAR)
areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: Pharmacology Education Project and Core Concepts of Pharmacology
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: IUPHAR describes an international pharmacology education project and a global consensus list of core pharmacology concepts developed with educators from 22 countries across six continents.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Pharmacology is an established biomedical learning/practice area, not simply a role title or a country-specific pathway.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: All pharmacology occupations being biomedical-science roles; clinical practice and protected titles remain jurisdiction-dependent.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: About ISCB / What We Do
areas_of_specialization_evidence.locator: ISCB describes a worldwide community dedicated to advancing understanding of living systems through computation; its field coverage includes computational biology and bioinformatics.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Bioinformatics/computational biology is an established cross-disciplinary field that can be a Biomedical Science specialization when the work is specifically biological/biomedical data and questions.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: A separate role or subgroup for every computational method, or placing generic IT/data occupations under Biomedical Science.

areas_of_specialization_evidence.publisher: International Union of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology (IUBMB)
areas_of_specialization_evidence.title: IUBMB About and Standards for Doctoral Degrees in the Molecular Biosciences

areas_of_specialization_evidence.supports: Biomedical research spans related molecular and cellular disciplines; it cautions against treating one narrow diagnostic taxonomy as the entire parent domain.
areas_of_specialization_evidence.claim_limit: These fields as a fixed list of student subgroups or the inclusion of all organismal/ecological science within Biomedical Science.

source_references.title: Radiation Protection and Safety in Medical Uses of Ionizing Radiation (IAEA Safety Standards Series No. SSG-46)
source_references.locator: Paras 2.91-2.93 and 2.126-2.127, PDF pages 50 and 60 in the opened document: defines medical radiation technologists as specially educated health professionals; distinguishes diagnostic radiology, radiation therapy and nuclear medicine; states specialty/subspecialty structures vary by State and further training may be required.
source_references.supports: Medical imaging/radiography is a distinct technical and safety practice area with modality-specific learning; it should not be merged into rehabilitation or laboratory diagnostics.
source_references.claim_limit: Radiation-safety guidance is not a complete radiography curriculum or global professional taxonomy; modalities and recognition vary across States. The cited training scope also covers medical radiation technology beyond diagnostic imaging, so this recommendation deliberately narrows the D068 area to diagnostic imaging/radiography.

source_references.claim_limit: International professional guidance, not a legally binding global scope; national titles, regulation and which tests may be performed vary. It does not prescribe the D068 parent or area count.

source_references.title: CMI Professional Standard
source_references.locator: The standard organizes manager/leader capabilities under Personal Effectiveness, Interpersonal Excellence and Organisational Performance, and describes capability progression across career levels.
source_references.supports: Management is a capability set spanning personal, interpersonal and organizational performance dimensions; role seniority is a progression dimension, not necessarily a separate specialization.
source_references.claim_limit: A globally binding professional taxonomy or a claim that CMI's UK professional recognition applies internationally.

source_references.title: The EFQM Model
source_references.locator: EFQM describes its organization model through Direction (purpose/strategy), Execution (how the organization delivers), and Results (performance and intended outcomes).
source_references.supports: Strategic direction, execution/processes and organizational results are distinct cross-functional management concerns that can inform a plain-language internal specialization structure.
source_references.claim_limit: These three model dimensions as job titles, academic disciplines, or a prescribed count of General Management subgroups.

source_references.title: ISCO-08 � International Standard Classification of Occupations
source_references.locator: ISCO-08 is a hierarchical classification of jobs into occupational groups. ILO methodology explains that manager groups are distinguished by functional specialization and recommends using actual main tasks/duties, not organization size, to distinguish manager categories.
source_references.supports: The current subgroup records should be recognized as occupational classification buckets; actual tasks matter, and job titles or seniority do not establish a learning specialization.
source_references.claim_limit: ISCO groupings as student-facing areas of specialization or proof that every listed role belongs to General Management.

source_references.title: ISO 21502:2020 Project, programme and portfolio management � Guidance on project management
source_references.locator: ISO 21502 applies to project management across public, private and charitable organizations and project types; it treats general management only within the project-management context and is separate from programme and portfolio guidance.
source_references.supports: Project management is a distinct cross-sector professional practice and a neighboring catalogue domain, not automatically a General Management specialization.
source_references.claim_limit: Placing all project/programme managers in General Management or assigning certification requirements.

source_references.title: ISO 9001:2026 Quality management systems � Requirements
source_references.locator: ISO describes a globally recognized, sector-neutral quality-management system covering organizational context, leadership, planning, support, operations, performance evaluation and improvement; certification is optional and applies to organizational systems, not individuals.
source_references.supports: Quality, process control, performance evaluation and continual improvement are recognizable cross-sector organizational management practices.
source_references.claim_limit: ISO 9001 as an individual professional certification or proof that a quality manager belongs in General Management rather than a specialized sector/function domain.

source_references.publisher: United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)
source_references.title: Recommendation concerning the Status of Higher-Education Teaching Personnel
source_references.locator: UNESCO calls the 1997 Recommendation the only global standard-setting instrument dedicated specifically to higher-education teaching personnel and describes its scope as people engaged to teach, undertake scholarship or research, or provide educational services to students or the community.
source_references.supports: Teaching, scholarship/research and educational service are distinct but related higher-education functions; this parent is not ordinary school-level teaching by definition.
source_references.claim_limit: A fixed four-area taxonomy, exact role placements, or national qualification equivalence.

source_references.title: Number of classroom teachers and academic staff
source_references.locator: UIS defines tertiary academic staff around primary assignments in instruction and/or research and notes academic-rank and leadership titles are counted only when their principal activity is instruction or research.
source_references.supports: Education level and principal activity matter when separating academic roles from general school leadership or university administration.
source_references.claim_limit: A complete higher-education occupational taxonomy or a claim that every dean is academic staff.

source_references.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)
source_references.title: Resourcing Higher Education — Human resources in higher education
source_references.locator: OECD describes a continuum from academic roles to professional/administrative roles supporting teaching, research and engagement; it notes role mixes differ by institution and system.
source_references.supports: Academic teaching/research and professional services are distinguishable role contexts; education institutions and national systems vary.

source_references.title: Quality assurance in higher education
source_references.locator: UNESCO describes quality assurance as supporting access to higher-education learning, academic standards and qualification credibility, with work at institutional and system levels and respect for institutional diversity/autonomy.
source_references.supports: Quality assurance and institutional academic standards are meaningful governance/quality functions within higher education.

source_references.title: Number of classroom teachers and academic staff
source_references.locator: UIS defines tertiary academic staff around primary assignments in instruction and/or research and notes academic-rank and leadership titles are counted only when their principal activity is instruction or research.
source_references.supports: Education level and principal activity matter when separating academic roles from general school leadership or university administration.
source_references.claim_limit: A complete higher-education occupational taxonomy or a claim that every dean is academic staff.

areas_of_specialization.label: Student Learning, Academic Services and Community Engagement
areas_of_specialization.description: Provide learning-related services and support to students or communities and connect institutional teaching/research to public engagement where these are core higher-education functions.
